fact: The Tree of Peace of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy: by tradition, the founding nations buried their weapons beneath one.
The state tree of Maine, since 1945, and of Michigan, since 1955.
A member of the pea family, but one of the few that forms no nodules on its roots; most sources say it fixes no nitrogen.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service)

fact: When Dutch elm disease killed the elms that shaded so many American streets, the thornless form became one of the most planted trees to replace them.
The state tree of New Jersey, since 1950, and the provincial tree of Prince Edward Island, since 1987.
source: New Jersey Forest Service; Oregon State University; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Like every oak in the red oak group, it takes two summers to ripen its acorns. White oaks ripen theirs in one.
First brought to North America in 1756, as seedlings sent from England to the Philadelphia botanist John Bartram.
source: UVM Libraries, UVM Trees exhibit; Fire Effects Information System

fact: Where it meets bur oak the two cross, and the hybrid has a name of its own: Schuette's oak, Quercus × schuettei.
Not every one is blue. Wild trees run from dull green to silvery blue, and the bluest in yards are grafted selections such as 'Hoopsii'.
The state tree of Rhode Island.
Its wilted or dried leaves, fallen after a storm or a pruning, are poisonous to horses.
Its range is split among several subspecies. One, the Corsican pine of Corsica and southern Italy, is a leading timber tree in Britain and France.
The name probably comes from the short, slender twigs that stick out like pins along its trunk and larger limbs; others trace it to the small pin knots those leave in its lumber.
Its lower branches often hold their dead brown leaves through the winter.
The state tree of four states: Vermont, New York, West Virginia and Wisconsin.
Its sap runs when freezing nights alternate with thawing days, which is why sugaring season falls at the end of winter.
Probably the first North American tree grown in Europe: one brought back from the St. Lawrence by Jacques Cartier's expedition is said to have grown for years in the royal garden at Fontainebleau.
The provincial tree of Manitoba, since 1991, and, as Black Hills spruce, the state tree of South Dakota, since 1947.
source: Government of Manitoba; State Symbols USA

fact: By long tradition the national tree of the Czech Republic and of Slovakia, though it is not among the Czech constitution's official symbols.
source: Wikipedia; Czech and Slovak Museum and Library

fact: The Christmas tree in London's Trafalgar Square is a Norway spruce, sent by the city of Oslo every year since 1947 in thanks for Britain's help in the Second World War.
Trees are male or female. The female's seeds have a fleshy coat that smells of rancid butter when it falls and rots, which is why almost all planted ginkgos are male.
Its soft, light, even-grained wood is a favorite of woodcarvers.
The state tree of New Hampshire and the provincial tree of Saskatchewan.
source: State Symbols USA; Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan; NC State Extension

fact: One parent of the London planetree, the street tree of so many cities; the other is the oriental planetree of southeastern Europe and western Asia.
It spreads by suckers from its roots, so one planted tree can become a thicket. That, with seed, is how it escapes into fields and woods.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service); NC State Extension

fact: A leaf-mining moth first found near Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia in 1984 has spread across Europe since, browning its leaves by midsummer.
The Major Oak in Sherwood Forest, by legend Robin Hood's shelter, was reckoned 800 to 1,100 years old. In 2026 it was reported dead, and is being left standing.
source: Visit Sherwood; Woodland Trust Ancient Tree Inventory; Wikipedia

fact: The state tree of Louisiana.
The state tree of Oregon.
Scotland's national tree, by public vote in 2014.
The state tree of Oklahoma.
source: Oklahoma State University Extension; State Symbols USA

fact: The state tree of Connecticut, Illinois and Maryland.
The state tree of Pennsylvania.
The state tree of Indiana, Kentucky and Tennessee.
Almost every one planted in the West until the 1990s came from two lots of seed that reached Harvard's Arnold Arboretum early in 1948, which it sent out to gardens around the world.
Botanists have moved it between four genera, Cupressus, Chamaecyparis, Xanthocyparis and Callitropsis, and still do not agree which it belongs in.
The state tree of Missouri and Virginia, and the state flower of North Carolina and Virginia.
It was Kentucky's state tree from 1976 to 1994, when the tulip poplar got the title back.
source: Wikipedia; Kentucky Revised Statutes 2.095; University of Kentucky

fact: Despite its common name, mountain ash is not an ash: it is in the rose family, with apples and cherries.
The provincial tree of New Brunswick, proclaimed in 1987.
The state tree of Minnesota, where it is called Norway pine.
Never a dominant tree of the forest: it grows scattered among sugar maple, beech and other hardwoods and seldom forms pure stands.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

fact: Its flowers open from late summer, among the last nectar of the year for bees and hoverflies, and its black berries, rich in fat, ripen through the winter as food for blackbirds and thrushes.
On Ohio stream bottoms made too acid by coal-mine drainage for other bottomland trees, it is the tree that moves in and takes over. It is planted to reclaim strip mines.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Built for floods: in one study its seedlings survived 30 days under water, growing new roots from the drowned stem.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Apple orchards plant crabapples among their trees as pollinizers: most apples cannot set fruit with their own pollen, and a crab in bloom at the same time supplies it.
Crabapples serve as rootstocks for orchard apples. Siberian crabapple roots, for one, give the trees grafted on them the cold hardiness to fruit in the far north.
In Europe elms now survive mostly as suckers from old roots, which grow into small trees until elm bark beetles find them and Dutch elm disease kills them back.
The elms along the Mall in New York's Central Park are one of the largest and last remaining stands of American elm in North America.
The Canadian city of Saskatoon takes its name from the Cree word for the fruit of one serviceberry, misâskwatômina.
On the prairies its berries were a main ingredient of pemmican, the Indigenous food of dried meat and fat.
Ash belongs to the olive family, with olives and lilacs.
Its tough, shock-resistant wood is sought for tool handles, oars and baseball bats, and also goes into electric guitars and drum shells.
It arises naturally where red and silver maples meet, but the many named forms sold for streets and gardens are nursery selections.
Many animals eat its acorns, ducks especially. Its hard, strong wood is usually cut and sold simply as white oak, for furniture, flooring and barrels.
source: Silvics of North America; Fire Effects Information System

fact: Its leaves turn butter-yellow, sometimes orange, in autumn.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

fact: Planted far from its Rocky Mountain home, it has escaped from plantings in several northeastern states, Maine and New York among them.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

fact: Young trees are pyramidal, but old ones round off into a broad dome.
The usual wood for the ribs, gunwales and other main parts of a birchbark canoe.
The northernmost tree in North America, reaching just past 69°N in the delta of the Mackenzie River.
Aachen's Forster Linde, a littleleaf linden, is thought to be about 1,000 years old, though no old linden can be dated exactly: their hearts rot away, taking the rings with them.
Most of Stradivari's violin tops, a 2026 tree-ring study found, were Norway spruce grown high in the Alps, where the cold made for many narrow rings.
In Korea it is the classic village guardian tree, planted at the heart of villages for protection, and many old ones are protected as natural monuments.
Besides Dutch elm disease, it resists the elm leaf beetle, an insect that strips the leaves of elms.
Bees make an excellent, mildly spicy honey from its flowers.
Long thought extinct in the wild. A few stands in China may be wild survivors, but nearly every ginkgo descends from trees people planted.
Its sap is sweet, but sugarmakers seldom tap it: it is usually less sugary than sugar maple's, so takes more boiling, and its buds break early, which cuts the season short.
Its seeds often lie in the ground a full extra year, sprouting only in the second spring after they fall.
source: Woody Plant Seed Manual (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Pure stands of paper birch burn far less often than the mixed forest around them, only in unusually dry years.
source: USDA Forest Service Climate Change Tree Atlas

fact: Its two North American species are northern white cedar and western redcedar; the others grow in Korea, Japan and China.
The popular hedge 'Green Giant' can grow 3 to 4 feet a year in good conditions.
Once widely planted as a city shade tree, it has largely given way to the London planetree, which resists the leaf disease anthracnose that disfigures it.
Named for Jean Robin, herbalist to King Henry IV of France. A black locust in Paris's Square René-Viviani, said to have been planted by him around 1601, is the oldest tree in the city.
It reached western Europe by way of Constantinople in 1576, as seed sent to the botanist Clusius in Vienna; its wild home is the mountains of Greece and Albania.
Larches dominate the boreal forests of Siberia and Canada. They are Russia's most abundant trees, the main tree on over a third of its forest land.
source: Abaimov, Permafrost Ecosystems: Siberian Larch Forests (Springer, 2010)

fact: There are about 13 larches, all in the northern hemisphere; in North America and Siberia they reach the edge of the tundra.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Wikipedia; Silvics of North America

fact: Gall wasps make it grow dozens of kinds of gall, among them the oak apple, a spongy ball that a tiny wasp makes the tree grow from a bud.
The oldest known, along the Black River in North Carolina, is at least 2,624 years old: the oldest living tree in eastern North America.
source: Wikipedia; University of Arkansas (Stahle et al. 2019)

fact: Its acorns are the largest of any native oak, hence macrocarpa, large fruit.
source: USDA Forest Service, Silvics of North America

fact: It bears good acorn crops only every two or three years. The glut is more than squirrels, deer and jays can eat, so some acorns survive to sprout: a strategy called masting.
Lombardy poplar, its columnar form, grows fast but is short-lived: from about 40 or 50 years old it sheds branches and blows over easily.
Its species, the black poplar, is one of Britain's rarest native trees: only about 7,000 grow wild there, and only some 600 of them are female.
Many hawthorns set seed without pollination, each copying itself, so the genus splinters into near-identical lines. Counts of its species run from about 140 to over 1,000.
Its wood seldom rots, so farmers planted it for fence posts. It was tried, less successfully, for railroad ties.
The tallest on record, near Little Rock, Washington, stood about 330 feet, with a trunk six feet across.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

fact: The poet Wordsworth preferred the Scots pine of the Highlands to every other tree but the oak, for its beauty in winter, by moonlight and in the evening.
Its place as a nut and timber tree may one day be taken by hybrids with blight-resistant Asian chestnuts.
Big American chestnuts planted by settlers still grow in the West, in Sherwood, Oregon, for one, beyond the reach of the blight that killed the eastern trees.
Its nuts make up about a tenth of the eastern fox squirrel's diet.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Even its ground shells are put to use: as a non-slip agent in tires, to blast off paint, and in smokestack scrubbers.
source: Fire Effects Information System (USDA Forest Service)

fact: Its nectar sits too deep for short-tongued bees; long-tongued bees do its pollinating, among them the southeastern blueberry bee, a specialist of redbuds.
Its bark was once a main source of tannin for tanning leather.
Maryland's Wye Oak, the largest white oak in the United States and reckoned some 450 years old, fell in a thunderstorm in June 2002.
source: Maryland Department of Natural Resources; Wikipedia

fact: Native Americans hollowed its trunks into dugout canoes so often that early settlers west of the Appalachians called it canoewood. A big one could carry twenty people.
Besides heat and drought, it stands city air, pollution and compacted soil, which makes it a good street tree.
The first living tree known to science grew beside a village shrine in Hubei, where villagers called it shui-shan, water fir.
It is one of the most important commercial hardwoods of the Southeast.
Its wood goes into furniture, crates and plywood veneer, and once went into the cabinets of radios, televisions and phonographs.
source: Wikipedia; NC State Extension; Silvics of North America

fact: Its catkins are the most important food of ruffed grouse from late fall to early spring.
Deer seldom browse it, which helps it hold its own in woods full of deer.
Its nuts feed a long list of animals: black bears, deer, wild turkeys, ruffed grouse, raccoons, foxes, squirrels and porcupines among them.
It takes hard pruning so well that it is called hedge maple, and its leaves shrink when clipped, which makes it a favorite for bonsai.
Nurseries can graft it onto ash roots.

The emerald ash borer, the beetle killing North America's ashes, was found in white fringetrees in Ohio in 2014 and Illinois in 2015. Of three non-ash trees tested, it was the only one the beetle could grow up in.
Its leaves, boiled with iron sulphate, give a black dye.
The largest North American birch.
The provincial tree of Quebec.
To many noses its flowers smell of rotting fish.
Its fast growth and tight, upright forks make 'Bradford' trees prone to splitting apart in storms and under ice.
Copper beeches, its purple-leaved form, arose as natural mutants in several parts of Europe, and were known in Germany before 1488.
It flowers in fall, mostly in October and November, as its leaves turn yellow.
Most varieties bear better with another variety blooming nearby to give them pollen.
source: NC State Extension; Ontario Ministry of Agriculture

fact: Its flowers open before the leaves, making it one of the first nectar sources for bees in spring, and maples feed the caterpillars of the imperial moth.
Its roots run shallow and far: they lift driveways and sidewalks and find their way into septic systems and drains.
Its seeds are spread mainly by birds, and big crops come only every three to five years.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its small fruits are edible, mild raw or cooked, and can be made into jelly or tea; birds and squirrels eat them through the winter.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the gray hairstreak, red-spotted purple and viceroy butterflies.
It stands clay, dry and alkaline soils and road salt, so it is often planted along North American streets.
Its flowers draw butterflies and even hummingbirds, and deer usually leave it alone.
The name catalpa comes from the Muscogee (Creek) name for the tree, kutuhlpa, "winged head".
In Japan it is ōyamazakura, the "great mountain cherry", for flowers larger than the common mountain cherry's, and also beni-yamazakura, "red mountain cherry", for their deeper color.
Its pea-sized cherries ripen purple-black in summer and are too bitter to eat off the tree.
Long grown in its native southeastern Europe, it is still raised for timber in Bulgaria and Romania.
Its wood is white, hard and strong, used for furniture and turning, and prized for musical instruments, harps above all.
It belongs to the cashew family, with mango, pistachio, sumac and poison ivy, and its resinous sap can give a rash to people sensitive to poison ivy.
Its nutlets feed songbirds, wild turkeys and quail, and the witches'-brooms common on its branches shelter many insects.
Its soft wood turns easily, and was made into spools, clothespins and other small woodenware.
Its twigs are winter browse for snowshoe hare, moose and white-tailed deer, and in Maine its thickets hide bobcats and hares.
Canada's oldest known tree was one of these, in the Caren Range of British Columbia: about 1,800 years old when it was felled in 1980.
Its light, soft wood goes mostly to pulp and particleboard, and into matches, chopsticks, pallets and hockey sticks.
It is a favorite food of the spongy moth, whose caterpillars can strip it bare; a stand weakened that way often dies of root rot after.
Its acorns feed squirrels and birds, and its leaves the caterpillars of the imperial moth and banded hairstreak.
Its acorns are edible once their bitter tannins are leached or boiled out.
Its many named forms run from 'Densiformis', a mound 3 to 4 feet tall, to 'Hicksii', a column up to 20 feet, raised at Hicks Nurseries on Long Island.
It is poisonous to horses, dogs and cats as well as people, yet birds eat its red arils and spread the seeds.
Its sap is sugary, and the Plains peoples boiled it into syrup, though it is less sweet than sugar maple's.
Its young saplings, with three ragged leaflets, are often mistaken for poison ivy; boxelder's leaves grow in opposite pairs, poison ivy's one at a time.
One of the few trees that colors well even in shade, though more softly than in sun.
Described in 1901, it was not brought into cultivation until 1923, and is still hard to find in nurseries.
It and one other species make up a family of their own, whose fossils go back to the last age of the dinosaurs, in North America, Europe and Asia.
Trees are male or female. The males flower before the leaves come out, the females as they open; both flowers are small and easy to miss.
Both its names mean alder: clethra is the Greek for alder, alnifolia "with leaves like alder's". Another old name is white alder, though the two are not related.
It is often planted along streams and ponds to hold the banks against erosion, as it stands both short floods and short droughts once settled.
Its fruit is edible: the sweet pulp tastes something like ripe persimmon, the rind is tough and bitter, and it is sometimes made into wine. Most are left for the birds.
Rutgers University crossed it with the native flowering dogwood to breed disease-resistant hybrids, Cornus × rutgersensis.

The grove on Longwood Mall in Brookline, Massachusetts, planted by David Sears in the 1840s, is thought to be the oldest stand of European beeches in the United States; beech leaf disease now threatens it.
Its strong, shock-resistant wood is sold together with white ash's as "white ash", for tool handles, baseball bats and electric guitar bodies.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Tadpoles feed on leaves that fall into ponds, and ash leaves suit them well; red maple leaves, now replacing ash in many woods, slow tadpoles' growth, a Michigan study found.
Its leaves are among the biggest of any North American tree: doubly divided, up to 3 feet long and 2 feet wide.
Wild turkeys eat its seeds, and its leaves feed the caterpillars of the witch hazel dagger moth.
Each variety needs a set number of winter chilling hours, so the right one depends on where it is grown.
It harbors crown rust, a fungus that attacks oats, and is the main winter host in North America of the soybean aphid, a pest of soybeans.
It leafs out before the native shrubs and shades them out, and its rich leaf litter feeds invasive European earthworms, which strip the forest floor bare.
Its worst enemy is the spruce budworm, which prefers it to spruce despite the name; three years' defoliation in an outbreak can kill three-quarters of a tree's fine roots.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Once dismissed by loggers as a weed tree, it is now one of the most important commercial softwoods of the West.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: It is host to two parasitic mistletoes, and the swellings dwarf mistletoe raises on its trunk weaken the lumber cut from it.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Its name griseum, "gray", probably refers to the silvery undersides of its leaves, not its coppery bark.
Its bark peels back in papery cinnamon curls that stay on the tree rather than falling.
Its heavy wood is used for furniture, cabinets and millwork, and is usually sold with yellow birch, not told apart.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the mourning cloak butterfly, and a leafcutter bee cuts pieces from them to line its nest.
Box Hill in Surrey is named for it: the hill holds the largest native box woodland in England.
The box tree moth, from East Asia, settled in Europe in 2007, and its caterpillars now strip boxwoods across the continent.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the hackberry emperor and question mark butterflies.
It is very drought-hardy: in southeastern South Dakota, 96% of hackberries survived the Dust Bowl years of 1934 to 1939.
Its other names include Kentucky yellow-wood, virgilia and gopherwood.
Prune it only in summer: cut in winter or spring, it bleeds sap heavily.
Its other old names are snowdrop-tree and opossum-wood.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its soft, close-grained wood is a favorite for crafts; squirrels eat its seeds, and bees make honey from its flowers.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Its thick, corky bark gives it the name cork tree, though it is no relation of the cork oak.
Trees are male or female, and only the females bear the black fruits that birds carry off; it is now listed as invasive in Illinois, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia.
Its fruit is edible raw and made into jelly, and the juice was once used to flavor rum and brandy, which gives it the name rum cherry.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: First planted near Paris in 1623, and widely in western and central Europe in the 1900s, it has run wild and is now one of Europe's worst invasive trees.
Widely planted in northern North America, it has run wild in parts of Canada and the northern United States.
Its name pseudocamellia means "false camellia", and in Japanese it is natsutsubaki, "summer camellia".
In Japan it is also called shara: from the 1700s it stood in at temples for the sal tree, sacred in Buddhism, which does not grow there.
The purple lilac is New Hampshire's state flower, chosen as "symbolic of that hardy character of the men and women of the Granite State".
From 1876 Victor Lemoine's nursery in Nancy, France, carried on by his son and grandson, introduced more than 200 named lilacs, many still sold today.
source: Library and Archives Canada (Montreal Botanical Garden); Wikipedia

fact: A fir in the Caucasus was known before 1800, but it was taken for the European silver fir until Alexander von Nordmann's visit showed it was a species of its own.
It grows wild in mountain forests around the eastern Black Sea, between 900 and 2,100 m, where winters are cold and rain plentiful.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

fact: In Minoh, near Osaka, its autumn leaves are fried in a sweet batter as momiji tempura, a local specialty.
Carl Peter Thunberg described it from Japan in the 1780s, naming it for its hand-shaped leaves; it reached England in 1820.
source: Wikipedia; Trees and Shrubs Online; Oregon State University

fact: It takes heavy clipping, and is the classic hedge of formal gardens, such as the bosquets of Versailles.
Its wood made butchers' chopping blocks and piano hammers, and it burns well, as firewood and as charcoal.
Ise Grand Shrine, Shinto's holiest, is rebuilt every 20 years from hinoki grown in Kiso, where the trees are called go-shinboku, "divine trees".
Its wood keeps a strong, pleasant scent for years; the oil from it goes into perfumes, soaps and incense.
Its fruits feed at least eleven kinds of birds, black bears, chipmunks, deer and rabbits, and beavers eat its branches near water.
It is prone to golden canker, a fungus that kills branches, especially when heat or drought stresses the plant.
Its name mas, Latin for "male", contrasts it with a "female" dogwood of weaker wood.
Its tart, olive-shaped red fruits are edible, and best made into jelly.
Because it does not sucker, it is used as a single-stemmed rootstock for grafting the common hazel.
It is also called Turkish or Constantinople hazel, and it makes a tough, drought-tolerant street tree.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: It came to North America as an ornamental in the late 1800s, and by the early 1900s was planted across the Great Plains and the Southwest.
source: NC State Extension; Fire Effects Information System

fact: Its small silvery-yellow flowers, very fragrant, open in early summer.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online; Wikipedia

fact: Oregon bans its sale as a noxious weed, and Washington joined it in 2025.
source: Oregon Administrative Rules 603-052-1200; Washington State Department of Agriculture; Wikipedia

fact: Its late, nectar-rich flowers draw bees and migrating monarch butterflies in September, and in North America hummingbirds too.
It reached Western gardens through the 1980 Sino-American Botanical Expedition, whose plants went to the Arnold Arboretum.
Its genus honors Richard Kolkwitz, a Berlin professor of botany, and amabilis means "lovely".
Wilson sent its seed to Veitch Nurseries in Exeter, England, where it first flowered in 1910, nine years later.
It is the favorite food of the spicebush swallowtail, whose young caterpillars look like bird droppings and hide in leaves they fold shut with silk.
Another name is wild allspice, and its young leaves and twigs make a spicy tea.
Its other names include sweetbay, swamp magnolia and beaver tree.
Its black seeds hang out of the ripe pink fruit on threads, in a thin red coat; birds swallow them, digest the coat and drop the seeds elsewhere.
Its catkins fling out their pollen at more than half the speed of sound, one of the fastest movements known in plants.
source: Taylor et al. 2006, Sexual Plant Reproduction; Trees and Shrubs Online; Wikipedia

fact: Its bark fibers, with paper mulberry's, went into the earliest paper money, in Tang dynasty China.
In Okinawa its fibers are woven into a cloth called bashōfu.
Its yellowish flowers, which W. J. Bean called "of no beauty", open a cluster at a time over a long season.
It has many other names: black gum, sour gum, pepperidge, beetlebung and snag tree among them.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

fact: Its small flowers are rich in nectar and a major source of wild honey; beekeepers once used its hollow trunks as hives, called bee gums.
It is also sold as Japanese andromeda, from the genus it used to be placed in.
Its drooping clusters of white bell flowers give it another name, lily-of-the-valley shrub.
It is one of the most widely planted trees in the northern United States and Canada.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service)

fact: Like other cherries, its leaves, stems and seeds are poisonous to dogs, cats and horses.
Its small dark fruits are edible, though strong-tasting, and birds take them.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the giant swallowtail, North America's largest butterfly.
Its flowers smell unpleasant, which earns it the name stinking ash.
Its acorns take two seasons to ripen, and their kernels are very bitter.
Squirrels, deer and blue jays eat its acorns, and wood ducks and the endangered Kirtland's warbler nest in its trunk cavities.
It is called cow oak because cattle eat its large, sweet acorns, as do deer, squirrels, hogs and black bears.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: It is also called basket oak: its wood splits into long, thin, flexible strips for weaving baskets.
source: Silvics of North America (US Forest Service); Wikipedia

fact: Its dried, ground leaves are filé powder, which thickens and flavors Louisiana gumbo.
Its root was one of the earliest exports from North America to Europe; English ships sailed in 1603 just to fetch it.
It is endangered in Canada, where it grows only in southwestern Ontario, and critically imperiled in Vermont.
It is named for Richard Maack, a 19th-century Russian naturalist and explorer who found it in the Amur River valley, on the border of Siberia and China.
Its pea-like flowers smell of vanilla, and its flat seed pods, 2 to 4 inches long, follow in fall.
It is rare in the wild: its trees grow far apart and set few good seeds.
Butterflies and hummingbirds visit its flowers, and birds and small mammals eat its red seeds.
It is named for John Fraser (1750–1811), the Scottish plant collector who explored these mountains.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: The balsam woolly adelgid, an invasive insect first recorded in its wild stands in 1957, has devastated them, and the species is now listed as endangered.
David Douglas found it near the mouth of the Columbia River in 1825, and later brought it into British gardens.
Its lumber goes into framing, flooring and paper.
It reached Japan in the early 1700s, and its Japanese name, tōkaede, means "Chinese maple".
Its species name honors Heinrich Bürger, a 19th-century German botanist.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: In Japan and elsewhere it is grown as bonsai.
Pruning can make it a single-trunked small tree or a many-stemmed shrub, and it is one of the hardiest maples, best where summers are cool.
The Morton Arboretum near Chicago selected a dense, even form, 'Morton', sold as State Street maple.
The botanist Kingo Miyabe found it on a stop during a train ride; it was described in 1888 and reached Germany the same year.
source: Oregon State University; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Its timber is sold with sugar maple's as "hard maple".
Small leafy stipules at the base of each leaf stalk tell it from sugar maple.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: In Britain it is known simply as sycamore, and also as great maple and harewood, the name its wood is sold under for veneer.
Its pale, odorless wood has long been the choice for kitchenware such as cutting boards and bowls, and its rare wavy-grained timber for violins.
It is also called purplebloom maple: its flowers have reddish-purple sepals around cream petals and open before the leaves.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Boone County Arboretum

fact: Another name for it is Keijo maple, after Keijō, the name Seoul went by under Japanese rule.
Its name is often misspelled Tartar or Tartarian maple.
It has escaped and become invasive in parts of the Midwest.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Its name truncatum, "cut off square", refers to the straight base of its leaves.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Crossed with Norway maple, it gave 'Keithsform', sold as Norwegian Sunset.
Its name pedatum, "like a bird's foot", describes how the frond forks.
It also grows in eastern Asia; Asa Gray counted it among the plants shared by Japan and North America.
Native Americans ate its seeds after roasting them and leaching out the poison in water for several days.
source: NC State Extension; Oregon State University; Wikipedia

fact: Its leaves resist disease better than other buckeyes'.
Its crushed leaves smell unpleasant, which gives it the names fetid buckeye and stinking buckeye.
source: Oregon State University; Wikipedia; NC State Extension

Its acorns feed woodpeckers, blue jays, wild turkeys, deer and black bears.
Also called Darlington oak, it is short-lived for an oak, about 50 years.
source: NC State Extension; Silvics of North America

fact: It stands drought and salt spray, which suits it to the sandy southern coast.
It was first described in 1788 by Thomas Walter, an English-born botanist in South Carolina.
It may be 30 years old before it bears its first acorns.
Its acorns are big, up to about 1.5 inches long, and sweet; wildlife eat them in the good years, which are infrequent.
source: Oregon State University; Silvics of North America; Wikipedia

fact: For years it went by Quercus prinus, the name the Forest Service's Silvics still uses; botanists dropped it because it could not be pinned to one species.
It honors Gotthilf Muhlenberg (1753–1815), a Lutheran pastor and amateur botanist in Pennsylvania; the umlaut often added to his name was Engelmann's mistake.
Oak wilt, a fungal disease, usually kills it within two to four years.
It is an important source of lumber and pulp, and bears heavy acorn crops every year.
Its acorns feed waterfowl, wild turkeys, woodpeckers, deer, black bears and squirrels.
source: NC State Extension; Fire Effects Information System; Wikipedia

fact: It was described in 1860 by Samuel Botsford Buckley, Texas's assistant state geologist, and named for his chief.

Oak wilt kills it within weeks of the first symptoms; the fungus spreads through grafted roots and by sap beetles.
'Crimson Spire' began as a chance seedling in a row of English oaks at Willet Wandell's nursery in Oquawka, Illinois, and was patented in 1995.
source: US Plant Patent 9103; International Oak Society

fact: From white oak it takes its resistance to powdery mildew and its rusty-red fall color; from columnar English oak, its narrow shape and toughness in the city.
source: Linda Hall Library Arboretum; Chicago Botanic Garden

fact: Its best-known form, 'Long', sold as Regal Prince, came from a 1975 seedling of columnar English oak crossed with swamp white oak, and was patented in 2002.
source: US Plant Patent 12673; University of Arkansas Extension

fact: It resists powdery mildew and borers and stands up to wind and ice.
Rhododendron is Greek for "rose tree".
Its flowers draw hummingbirds, butterflies and bees, and its thickets give winter cover.
Its leaves and bark, rich in tannin, were used to tan leather.
Its fruit can hang on until spring, and feeds wild turkeys, ruffed grouse, robins, flickers, raccoons and chipmunks.
source: Wikipedia; NC State Extension; Fire Effects Information System

fact: Only female plants bear the fuzzy red fruit clusters, which last into winter.
Pheasants, quail and wild turkeys eat its fruit, and its leaves feed the caterpillars of the luna moth and spring azure.
Goats eat it gladly: in one trial, goats browsing badly infested pastures all but wiped it out within four seasons.
Rose rosette, a disease spread by a tiny mite, kills many wild stands and is one of its few natural checks.
It has fern-like leaves, and its stems are coated with a purplish waxy bloom over slender prickles.
Its fruits are black with a bluish bloom, about five-eighths of an inch across.
Charcoal from its wood was important in making gunpowder, and its bark tanned leather.
source: Wikipedia; Trees and Shrubs Online (quoting Loudon)

fact: Its wood is light and tough but rots outdoors; kept dry, as roof rafters, it was said to last a hundred years.
source: Wikipedia; Trees and Shrubs Online (quoting Loudon)

fact: Linnaeus named it babylonica believing it was the willow of Babylon in the Psalms; that tree was in fact a poplar, and this one is Chinese.
source: NC State Extension; Oregon State University

fact: In humid climates willow anthracnose, a canker disease, makes it short-lived; even healthy trees live only 40 to 75 years.
Its biggest trees grow at the foot of mountains and in the oases of Inner Mongolia, where it is planted to shelter fields from desert winds.
Its Chinese name is said to mean "upside-down willow", from the belief that a cutting will root even planted the wrong way up.
It was first described in 1785 by Humphry Marshall, "the father of American dendrology".
It is the only native willow cut for timber, and its light wood was once used for artificial limbs.
source: Wikipedia; Silvics of North America; Fire Effects Information System

fact: Its genus name comes from the Greek sambuce, an ancient wind instrument: its pithy twigs were hollowed into whistles.
Its cooked berries go into pies, jellies and wine, but the plant is mildly poisonous, and unripe fruit is far more toxic than ripe.
Long grown in Britain, it is sometimes sown in the wild there by birds, and has become naturalized in a few places.
Botanists agree it is of hybrid origin, but not on its parents: some say rowan is among them, others that it comes wholly from wild service tree and whitebeams.
It has the largest genome of any plant studied up to 2020, 26.5 billion base pairs, about eight times a human's.
source: Wikipedia; Guinness World Records; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Its old-growth forests shelter the threatened northern spotted owl and the endangered marbled murrelet, a seabird that nests high in the trees.
The IUCN lists it as endangered, with fewer than 80,000 trees left in the wild.
Its old-growth wood is brittle: felled trees often shattered, and the wood went into fence posts, grape stakes, shingles and pencils.
source: Fire Effects Information System; Silvics of North America; Wikipedia

fact: It is a cross between rowan and the Swedish whitebeam, and carries four sets of chromosomes.
In southern England it is the most reliably showy of its group in autumn fruit; thrushes and waxwings eat the juicy berries and spread the seeds.
In gardens it is usually grafted; its forms include 'Fastigiata', with upright branches, and 'Leonard Springer', with larger fruit.
Its name refers to Thuringia, in central Germany.
Gardens grow it as named forms; the first to reach the West was the Chinese 'Fortunei', and 'Anthony Waterer' and 'Bumalda' came later.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Oregon State University

fact: It grows fast and seeds itself aggressively, so NC State Extension advises planting something else.
source: NC State Extension; Wikipedia (citing the National Invasive Species Information Center)

fact: Each pod holds one to three brown seeds that look like popcorn, and some sources count them edible.
Bees and butterflies take nectar from its flowers, and small mammals browse its leaves.
It reached France in 1747 and England in 1753, and it is planted as a street tree in Chinese cities such as Xi'an.
A dye made from it was used in old Japanese prints.
It was first brought to the West by the plant collector Richard Oldham in 1862.
Its hard wood was used for umbrella ribs and for the pieces of shogi, Japanese chess.
Many botanists treat it as a subspecies of the Japanese tree lilac, Syringa reticulata subsp. pekinensis.
Its flowers draw hummingbirds and butterflies, and songbirds shelter in it.
Its heavy, straight-grained, rot-resistant wood has gone into barrels, railroad ties and shingles.
Like baldcypress, where it grows in water it sends up woody "knees" from its roots, though less often.
Its genus name, Taxus, may come from the Greek toxon, a bow: its wood made the English longbow, and lutes too.
Birds eat the red arils and pass the poisonous seeds unharmed, which spreads the tree.
It reached the Jardin des Plantes in Paris in 1880, sent by Emil Bretschneider, and went on from there to Kew in 1904.
It reached British nurseries in 1913, through Veitch, from seed William Purdom collected in northern China.
Its copious nectar draws bees and butterflies, notably the white-letter hairstreak.
Where it meets littleleaf linden the two cross freely; the hybrid is the common lime of European avenues.
Its fragrant flowers hang in clusters of about seven under a leafy yellow-green bract, and bees pollinate them.
Its leaves are halfway between those of its parents, the large-leaved and small-leaved lindens.
It is the state tree of Massachusetts and North Dakota.
A few surviving trees have been selected and named as resistant clones, though how resistant they are varies.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Oregon State University

fact: Its form 'Morton', sold as Accolade, has resisted Dutch elm disease for more than 80 years and is much used in breeding.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Oregon State University

fact: Some of its forms are hardy to USDA zone 2, among the coldest of garden zones.
It was once also called wych hazel, a name that has since passed to the unrelated witch hazels.
Its name wych comes from an Old English word for pliant, the root of wicker; it was once used for other supple-branched trees too.
It is largely resistant to Dutch elm disease, Japanese beetles and elm leaf beetles, and has become important in breeding resistant elms.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online; Oregon State University

fact: It is often confused with the weak-wooded Siberian elm, which nurseries sometimes sell as "Chinese elm".
It is widely judged a poor ornamental, with weak branches and a messy habit, and leaf beetles often attack it.
source: NC State Extension; Oregon State University

fact: Some of its clones resist Dutch elm disease well, and it has been crossed with other elms in the United States and Italy to breed resistant trees.
source: Wikipedia; NC State Extension; Oregon State University

fact: It crosses in the wild with the introduced Siberian elm, which threatens its genetic integrity.
Its wood is counted inferior to American elm's, yet the two are often mixed and sold together as soft elm, for boxes, baskets, crates and barrels.
source: Silvics of North America; Fire Effects Information System

fact: Southern highbush blueberries are crosses of it with Darrow's blueberry, a native of the Southeast.
Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the brown elfin butterfly.
The viburnum leaf beetle, an invasive insect from Eurasia, can strip it bare.
Its fruit feeds songbirds, grouse, wild turkeys and squirrels, and deer browse its twigs and leaves.
It goes by many folk names, among them nannyberry, sheepberry, sweetberry, cowberry and nanny plum.
Crossed with blackhaw in gardens, it gave the hybrid Viburnum × jackii.
Its fruit is eaten raw and made into jam and preserves, as the Meskwaki and colonial settlers did.
source: NC State Extension; Oregon State University; Wikipedia

fact: It stands fire in the landscape, and gives good fall color.
Its name florida means "full of flowers".
source: NC State Extension; Oregon State University

fact: Hummingbirds and butterflies come to its flowers.
There are about 140 to 160 species, shrubs and small trees across the northern temperate world, with outliers in Africa and South America.
source: Wikipedia; NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: W. J. Bean, the great British authority, wrote that few groups have so many hardy species with so little garden value; the fruits, often abundant and reddish, are their best feature.
Its name is Greek for "rose tree". It is a huge genus, about 1,000 species in the heath family, most of them in eastern Asia and the Himalayas.
Azaleas are rhododendrons. Linnaeus kept them as a genus of their own, but botanists merged them into Rhododendron in 1836.
Botanists cannot agree how many yews there are: counts run from one widespread species, with the rest as subspecies, to more than 20, told apart largely by where they grow.
The cancer drug paclitaxel (Taxol) was first isolated in 1971 from the bark of the Pacific yew.
It is named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, for the many colors of its flowers. There are about 300 species.
Three irises gave statistics one of its most famous data sets: measurements of 150 flowers that Ronald Fisher used in a 1936 paper, now a standard test case in machine learning.
source: UCI Machine Learning Repository; Wikipedia (Iris flower data set)

fact: It is named for Pierre Magnol (1638–1715), the Montpellier botanist who first worked out the idea of plant families.
Its species grow in two widely separated regions: eastern and southeastern Asia, and the Americas, from the eastern United States south into South America.
Mulberries are not related to blackberries or raspberries: they belong to the fig family.
More than 200 species names have been published for mulberries since Linnaeus named seven, yet botanists accept fewer than 20 species.
Most spruce needles are four-sided and sit on tiny woody pegs that stay on the twig when the needles fall, so a bare spruce twig feels rough.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online; Wikipedia

fact: There are about 35 species, across the cool northern hemisphere. In the wild spruces tend to take the wetter sites, firs the drier.
There are about 70 to 100 species, across the temperate northern hemisphere, most of them in eastern Asia.
Its flowers are white, pink or red; the spring-flowering kinds are all white.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

fact: Its fruit, the haw, looks like a berry but holds one to five seeds, each in its own hard stone, like a cluster of tiny plums.
There are about 10 to 25 species, native to Europe, North Africa and Asia; none is native to the Americas.
The Callery pear first came to the United States to be tested by the Department of Agriculture as a rootstock for orchard pears.
There are only about a dozen species, all in the Old World, from southeastern Europe to eastern Asia. Lilacs are in the olive family, closest to privet.
Its leaves come in opposite pairs and are usually smooth-edged; in one species they are divided into leaflets.
There are about 350 to 400 species, on every continent but Australia and Antarctica, most of them in the cool north.
Each willow is male or female. Some are trees, but some arctic and alpine willows creep along the ground only a few inches high.
It is a big genus of over 200 species that includes not only cherries but almonds, apricots, peaches and plums: all stone fruits.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; Wikipedia; NC State Extension

fact: Many of its species carry cyanide-forming compounds, so their seeds, leaves and stems can poison people and pets even where the fruit is good to eat.
Its name is Latin, from cornu, "horn", for its very hard wood.
Some dogwoods ring their small flowers with large white or pink bracts that look like petals; others bear open clusters of small flowers. Some have edible fruit.
It is named for William Forsyth (1737–1804), the Scottish head of the royal gardens at Kensington Palace and a founder of the Royal Horticultural Society.
It belongs to the olive family. There are about 11 species, all in eastern Asia but one, which grows wild in southeastern Europe.
There are about 130 to 160 species, most of them in eastern Asia; only one, Acer laurinum of Indonesia, grows wild south of the equator.
Maples belong to the soapberry family; their closest relatives outside their own genus include the buckeyes and horse chestnuts.
There are 50 to 67 species, depending on the authority, across the northern hemisphere, from tall trees to ground-hugging shrubs. They are in the cypress family.
source: Wikipedia; NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online

fact: Birds and small mammals eat its fleshy, berry-like cones, blue to red, and spread the seeds.
Its parents, paperbark maple from China and Nikko maple from Japan and China, belong to a small group of maples whose leaves are split into three leaflets.
source: Trees and Shrubs Online; NC State Extension

fact: The Nikko maple parent is named for the botanist Carl Maximowicz, who found it in Japan in the 1860s, and for the Japanese town of Nikko.
source: NC State Extension; Trees and Shrubs Online
